_pattern_report: Yes, the batch felt exploitable, though not primarily through length. Option lengths were reasonably mixed and the key did not feel reliably longest. The dominant cross-item tell is hedging asymmetry: in nearly every set the option I picked was the qualified, two-sided, or conditional one (may, can, in some cases, without limiting, complicates rather than condemns, reframes rather than reverses), while distractors carried absolutes (invariably, only, all, any role at all, regardless, no meaningful effect). A second, higher-level tell is a shared rhetorical template repeated across items: many answers have the same speech-act shape of concede-then-qualify or recast-an-apparent-flaw-as-deliberate (items 5, 16, 17, 22, 23, 24 all reward essentially the same move), so a solver who learns that move on one item answers the rest without any passage. Third, several strengthen/weaken items are solvable by pure evidential logic because only one option is even the right kind of evidence (2, 6, 10, 15, 20). I answered all 24 with moderate-to-high confidence on most, which for a passage-based test is itself the finding.
